title: How to decide if a DIY super fund is right for you
full_text:
Younger investors are underpinning a fresh surge in new self-managed superannuation funds as more people seek to grab greater control of their retirement savings.
The latest Australian Taxation Office figures show more than 52,000 SMSFs were started last financial year, while only 5011 were closed, taking the total number to a record 680,301, up more than 12 per cent in two years.
More than $1.1 trillion currently sits in SMSFs, which have evolved beyond just a tool for wealthy savers and business owners, but financial advisers and even the sector’s peak body say they are not ideal for everyone.
Tribeca Financial head of advice Robert Devlin said the strongest force behind the recent SMSF popularity surge had been that more Australians were seeking control. “People want more say over where their super is invested and, as balances grow, they tend to become more engaged with it,” he said.
SMSF Association chief executive Peter Burgess said savers were seeking greater transparency, and the increase in compulsory super contributions to 12 per cent in recent years was helping to build bigger balances.
The most recent ATO statistics, from 2023-24, put the average super balance at almost $183,000, while recent numbers from financial regulator APRA show the average SMSF balance is $1.63m.
SMSFs can have up to six members, and more than two thirds of them have two members.
Overall SMSF member numbers have climbed 11.6 per cent to 1.25 million people since 2024.
“Australians’ attitudes towards superannuation are shifting dramatically,” Mr Burgess said.
“Three consecutive years of near-record SMSF growth, a trend we have never witnessed before, is clear evidence of this changing mindset.” While super cannot generally be accessed until after age 60, Mr Burgess said the statistics showed younger people were thinking about retirement and wealth planning earlier in life.
“In the June 2026 quarter, half of the new fund establishments were by members aged under 45,” he said.
Mr Devlin said property had been the big driver of SMSF growth in recent years. “The ability to directly own property through super has been a really tangible reason for people to look at an SMSF,” he said.
If you buy an investment property in a SMSF and hold it to retirement, then switch your super to a tax-free account-based pension; there is no capital gains tax payable.
This strategy was dealt a body blow in June when the Albanese government buckled to pressure from the Greens and banned people from borrowing within their SMSF to buy residential property, a backflip aimed at getting its controversial budget tax changes through parliament.
Mr Devlin said borrowing for property within super had not disappeared altogether, as the ban did not extend to commercial property.
“There’s still a strong use case for business owners wanting to own their commercial premises through their SMSF and potentially borrow to do it,” he said.
People can still buy residential real estate outright in their SMSF if they have enough cash in there, but the Labor backflip means that SMSFs without large balances can no longer do this.
Years ago, advisers used to say people needed at least $200,000 in super to make SMSFs worthwhile, but many now suggest bigger numbers.
“I don’t think there’s a magic age or balance,” Mr Devlin said. “As a general guide, somewhere around $400,000 to $600,000 is where the fixed costs can become easier to justify.” These costs can include fund administration, financial statements and tax returns, annual independent audits, potential investment fees and brokerage, ongoing advice, and company registration and ASIC fees in some cases.
JBS Financial Strategists chief executive Jenny Brown said accounting and audit fees could cost $2000-$3000 annually.
“A lot of people don’t realise that there’s a lot of fixed costs, and unless they’re prepared to do some or all of the work themselves, then they need to outsource it, and then often the costs can become the same as a platform,” she said.
“Our view is unless you really want to buy property in it, or do something like crypto, and I’m not recommending that, with smaller balances they just don’t stack up. If you’re going to buy a whole lot of direct shares, ETFs and term deposits, you can do that in a platform.
“If you’ve got in excess of $1m they do stack up, but if you’ve got under $500,000 my view is they don’t, unless you’re prepared to do the investments and administration yourself.” Ms Brown said that for people who wanted to be hands-on and have good balances, SMSFs could be great.
“Half of our clients have self-managed super funds, I love them, but they’re only for the right clients,” she said.
Mr Devlin said SMSFs “can be fantastic, but they shouldn’t be entered into lightly”.
“If you want more control, have enough scale and there’s a genuine investment or strategic reason for having an SMSF, then it can absolutely be worth considering,” he said.
“But I wouldn’t set one up just because you can. For a lot of people, the alternatives like retail or industry funds will suit them a lot better, even with larger balances.” A key reason for this was the responsibility, compliance and administration that came with DIY super, Mr Devlin said.
“And you need to think further ahead, particularly around liquidity as you get older,” he said.
Mr Burgess noted that “illiquid investments (such as property) could be problematic when it came time to pay out benefits”.
“SMSFs do not have the same access to government compensation arrangements for theft or fraud that apply to APRA-regulated funds,” he said.
“It’s important to weigh the benefits of greater control and flexibility against the associated costs and responsibilities. While an SMSF can be an effective retirement savings structure, its success depends on informed decisions, sound governance, and continued engagement.”
